alternative: Model the elements as a closed enum and write each operation as a function that matches over it: adding an operation is one new function, adding a variant is a compiler-generated to-do list (the compiler reports every match that must be updated), and no trait surgery or downcasting is involved. If node types must stay open to other crates, use a trait per operation with a provided traversal method plus a required hook (the shape of syn's Visit trait), or a data-types-a-la-carte encoding with trait objects and generics, instead of the visitor's subclass-and-re-dispatch protocol.
idiom_name: no implementation inheritance to extend a visitor: enum + match (closed set), or a trait with provided methods plus Any downcasting (open set, unergonomic)
implementation_notes: The pattern's mechanism is implementation inheritance plus a runtime type test, and Rust has neither: a trait cannot inherit another trait's implementation, a `dyn Visitor` cannot be re-dispatched through a subtype relation, and the only supported runtime test is Any::downcast_ref/downcast_mut, which requires Any as a supertrait and restricts visitors to 'static types. The C++ to Rust phrasebook states the situation plainly: the extension that handles both changing data and changing behaviour 'is possible to implement' by opting into RTTI with Any, but 'the ergonomics of the approach make other approaches more common'. What replaces it is an enum whose variants are the element kinds with each operation a free function that matches over it - exhaustiveness is compiler-checked (E0004), a new operation is one function, and a new variant is a list of matches the compiler hands you - and, for genuinely open type sets, trait objects where the operation trait provides a traversal method and a required per-node hook. Keep a visitor-shaped protocol only when a downstream crate must extend element types you do not control and you accept the downcast tax.
pitfalls: Any::downcast_ref succeeds only for the exact concrete type and only for 'static types: a visitor held as a trait object must be downcast to that object type, and the trait must declare Any as a supertrait - the usual source of 'no handler' surprises.

An enum is closed: adding a variant recompiles every match (safely, with the compiler listing them), which is the opposite of this pattern's promise, so do not pick the enum form when downstream crates must contribute variants.

Trait objects cannot carry generic methods or return Self, so a visitor trait can only accumulate through &mut self or name an associated result type - another reason the OO protocol translates poorly.
Boxing every element to keep a common base type costs an allocation and indirection per node, which a plain enum avoids entirely.
